Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Gameplay 2.1 Piece Movement 2.2 Peg Placement 3 Goal Overview In Thrive, you play as one of two lotus flowers, competing to control the pond. Be the first to capture all but one of your opponent's seed pods and win this game of tactical decision making! Gameplay On a player's turn, in this order, if they can, they must: 1.Move one of their pieces. 2.Then place 2 pegs in any of their pieces. Piece Movement All pegs in a piece other than the center peg represent the possible moves that piece can take, relative to its position on the board, (represented by its center peg). Every piece starts with one peg allowing the piece to move one space forward. When a piece is moved onto another piece, the other piece is removed from the game. Pieces can jump over other pieces. Pieces cannot move off the game board. Pieces do not rotate. Peg Placement Pegs have to be placed into empty holes in your own pieces, and only into pieces that have not yet been captured. You can place your two pegs on different pieces on the same turn. You do not need to place either of the pegs onto the piece you just moved. Goal If you reduce your opponent to just one piece remaining, you win the game. Secondary goal: In a game where both players have exactly two pieces remaining, a player may instead win the game by filling one of their remaining pieces with pegs. Thrive is a two-player abstract strategy game with incredibly simple rules that grows in complexity as you play.

You play as one of two lotus flowers, competing to control the pond. Be the first to capture all but one of your opponent’s seed pods and win this game of tactical decision making!

Each turn you move a piece, then add two additional pegs to any of your pieces, giving them more possibilities for movement on future turns.

—description from the publisher

[Rating: 4/10] Available on BGA tried it there. In theory this should be a game I like, but in practice it just isn't. I think it has to do with the arc of the game, most of the game will be just defending, unless inevitably either of players miss something, and than the game is over in a view moves.

[Rating: 4/10] An interesting chess-like abstract game, where you move one piece each turn, and increase the movement options of your pieces.  It ends up being a massive puzzle of making sure you protect your pieces while threatening to capture your opponent's pieces.    I still prefer Hive as my "chess alternative".  Also, the production of the player pieces is not great, so some pegs holes are barely wide enough to fit the pegs.  This issue made me drop my rating by 2 points.

[Rating: 5/10] Really wish I liked this game more. I really like the mechanics for evolving pieces and the layers that in can put into play. But I'm not sure they work in the game itself. Granted, I have not grasped the strategy of this game yet either, so it could just be a skill issue. But I'm not sure I really like it.

[Rating: 5/10] This abstract strategy was not my very favorite, sigh…why did I fall for the hotness back then?

[Rating: 5/10] This felt too much like chess. This means that I would often overlook threats. Also, losing a piece early in the game usually means you have no chance of winning.
